body:
Why Gujarat is important for understanding GIs

Gujarat has distinctive agricultural products and craft traditions whose identities are associated with particular localities. The state's registered geographical indications provide practical examples of how geographical origin can be important because of natural conditions, traditional workmanship or regional reputation.

The following examples appear as Registered in the official GI Registry's state-wise list of applications registered as on 31 March 2025. The list is a dated official record, not a claim about the total number or complete registration status of every product on 14 November 2026.

Important Gujarat GI examples

Registered GIGoods categoryAssociated region or product
Patan PatolaHandicraftTraditional Patola textile associated with Patan
Kutch EmbroideryHandicraftRegional embroidery associated with Kutch
Jamnagari BandhaniHandicraftTraditional tie-dyed textile associated with Jamnagar
Surat Zari CraftHandicraftZari craftsmanship associated with Surat
Sankheda FurnitureHandicraftTraditional furniture associated with Sankheda
Gir Kesar MangoAgriculturalMango associated with the Gir region
Bhalia WheatAgriculturalWheat associated with the Bhal region
Kachchhi KharekAgriculturalDate product associated with Kachchh

These entries show that GI protection is not restricted to handicrafts. Agricultural goods can also qualify when they satisfy the statutory geographical connection. Conversely, a traditional craft is not automatically protected merely because it has existed for generations; the relevant GI must meet the law's conditions and the goods must fall within its registered scope.

How GI recognition can help producers

GI recognition can help buyers distinguish genuine region-linked goods from misleading imitations. This distinction may support the reputation of skilled craft communities, agricultural producers and local enterprises.

The economic benefits are best understood as possibilities rather than guarantees. Better recognition can create opportunities for market access, improved demand and higher returns, but registration does not itself guarantee higher prices or income. Producers still require quality maintenance, suitable marketing, distribution arrangements and effective action against misleading use.

Maintaining the geographical identity

Registered product specifications and the declared geographical area matter. A seller cannot treat the GI as a general label for every similar-looking product. Producers and relevant organisations must protect the distinction between qualifying goods and imitations, including through appropriate checks on origin and product characteristics.

This is especially significant for handmade goods. A product manufactured elsewhere may imitate the appearance of a traditional textile without acquiring the geographical origin required for the registered indication.

A national example: Darjeeling Tea

Darjeeling Tea, associated with West Bengal, was India's first registered GI. The official GI register records its word application as application number 1 and its registration certificate as dated 29 October 2004. This example helps distinguish the year of the GI Act, the year it came into force and the year of the earliest registration.

Prelims focus

  • Patan Patola, Kutch Embroidery and Jamnagari Bandhani are Gujarat handicraft GI examples.
  • Gir Kesar Mango, Bhalia Wheat and Kachchhi Kharek are Gujarat agricultural GI examples.
  • Surat Zari Craft and Sankheda Furniture are recorded as handicraft GIs.
  • Darjeeling Tea was India's first registered GI; its word registration certificate is dated 29 October 2004.
  • Trap: GI recognition does not mean every similar product made outside the registered area can use that geographical indication.

[Sources: Geographical Indications Registry, Details of GI Applications Registered as on March 31, 2025, Gujarat entries, serial numbers 119–146, data status as on 31 March 2025 and consulted 14 November 2026; Geographical Indications Registry, Darjeeling Tea (Word), application 1, registration details, consulted 14 November 2026; NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class 11, 'Crafts Heritage', printed pp. 9–13; NCERT, Craft Traditions of India: Past, Present and Future, Class 12, 'Colonial Rule and Crafts', printed pp. 15–19; Intellectual Property India, Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999, sections 2, 11 and 22.]

pictures.alt: GI recognition helps distinguish genuine goods from imitations; possible buyer trust and livelihood gains require quality, marketing, distribution and enforcement.
pictures.caption: Legal recognition can support trust and livelihoods when genuine products reach buyers.

title: Geographical Indications of Gujarat: Products, Places and Rural Livelihoods

body:
Why plant varieties matter

Farmers grow different varieties of the same crop because those varieties may differ in yield, quality, maturity period, resistance to disease or adaptation to environmental conditions. A plant variety is an identifiable group of plants within a botanical taxon, distinguished by relevant characteristics and capable of being propagated consistently as a variety.

Crop improvement may involve selecting plants with desirable characteristics and using breeding methods to develop varieties that perform better under specified conditions. Better yield, disease resistance, improved quality and adaptation are common objectives. However, the usefulness of a variety alone is not sufficient for registration: the applicable legal criteria must also be satisfied.

India's special legislation

India enacted the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001, commonly abbreviated as the PPV&FR Act. It establishes a system for protecting eligible plant varieties while recognising the interests of farmers and plant breeders.

The Act provides for a Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Authority, a Plant Varieties Registry and a National Register of Plant Varieties. Under the Act, breeders, eligible farmers and other persons specified by law may seek registration of qualifying varieties.

The Act received assent on 30 October 2001. Its provisions were brought into force in stages: sections 2–13 and certain related provisions from 11 November 2005, and most remaining substantive provisions, including sections 14–94, from 19 October 2006. Thus, enactment and operational commencement should not be confused.

Types of varieties recognised by the framework

New varieties

A new variety must satisfy the legal requirements of novelty, distinctiveness, uniformity and stability. The criteria are commonly remembered as NDUS.

Extant varieties

An extant variety is an existing variety falling within the Act's definition, which includes specified notified varieties, varieties of common knowledge and farmers' varieties. For registration of an extant variety, the law provides for distinctiveness, uniformity and stability under the applicable regulations. It does not require the same novelty condition imposed on a new variety.

Farmers' varieties

A farmers' variety includes one traditionally cultivated and evolved by farmers in their fields, or a wild relative or landrace of common knowledge about which farmers possess common knowledge. Eligible farmers' varieties have a route to registration under the Act.

Essentially derived varieties

The Act also recognises essentially derived varieties, which are principally derived from another variety while retaining its essential characteristics, subject to statutory requirements. This category matters because creating a closely derived variety does not necessarily remove the rights and interests associated with the original variety.

The NDUS tests explained

  • Novelty: For a new variety, the breeder must satisfy the legal limits on earlier commercial disposal or sale of its propagating or harvested material.
  • Distinctiveness: The variety must be clearly distinguishable by at least 1 essential characteristic from any other variety whose existence is a matter of common knowledge in any country at the time of filing the application.
  • Uniformity: Its essential characteristics must be sufficiently uniform, allowing variation expected from its method of propagation.
  • Stability: Its essential characteristics must remain unchanged after repeated propagation or at the end of the relevant propagation cycle.

For the novelty test, section 15 generally uses a limit of 1 year in India before filing, 6 years outside India for trees and vines, and 4 years outside India for other crops, concerning sale or disposal by or with the consent of the breeder for exploitation. These limits do not mean that every previously sold variety becomes ineligible under every registration category; the distinction between new and extant varieties remains essential.

How registration works

An eligible applicant submits the prescribed application, identification of the variety and required particulars to the Registrar. Registration may involve examination, testing of essential characteristics, publication of the application and consideration of objections before a certificate is issued. The variety is identified by a denomination, meaning its formal variety name for registration and identification purposes.

Registration is not automatic for any plant. Applicants must comply with the category-specific requirements, and the Act imposes restrictions on registration of varieties falling within certain prohibited categories. In particular, varieties involving genetic use restriction technology or terminator technology cannot be registered.

Prelims focus

  • The PPV&FR Act was enacted in 2001.
  • Section 15 requires NDUS for registration of a new variety.
  • Extant varieties may be registered under the applicable DUS criteria without meeting the new-variety novelty requirement.
  • Distinctiveness concerns an essential characteristic separating the variety from any other variety of common knowledge.
  • The Act recognises farmers' varieties and essentially derived varieties.
  • Trap: An existing traditional variety and a newly developed variety do not necessarily face identical registration conditions.

[Sources: India Code, Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001, sections 1–3, 12–19 and 23; India Code, Act commencement notifications dated 11 November 2005 and 19 October 2006, consulted 14 November 2026; Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Authority, Plant Varieties Registry Forms, application categories, consulted 14 November 2026; NCERT, Science, Class 9, chapter 'Improvement in Food Resources', section 15.1.1, printed pp. 203–205; NCERT, Science, Class 8, 'Crop Production and Management', section 1.4, printed pp. 4–5.]

pictures.alt: New varieties require NDUS; extant varieties require DUS under applicable rules. Novelty is the extra test, while DUS is shared.
pictures.caption: New varieties require NDUS, while extant varieties are assessed under DUS criteria.

title: Plant Variety Protection: Registration and the NDUS Criteria

body:
Rights created by registration

Under section 28 of the PPV&FR Act, registration of a variety confers exclusive rights, subject to the Act, on the breeder or other entitled person to produce, sell, market, distribute, import or export the registered variety. The Act also provides for authorised agents and licensees.

A breeder is a person, group, farmer, institution or organisation that breeds, evolves or develops a variety in the manner recognised by the Act. A farmer who develops a registrable variety can therefore be protected as a breeder. The term is not restricted to a commercial seed company or a laboratory scientist.

Licensing and the seed system

A breeder may authorise other persons to produce or market a registered variety under the applicable legal conditions. This allows registered varieties to enter lawful seed production and distribution arrangements without requiring every producer to be the original breeder.

The registration system also provides for recording a variety's identity and characteristics. Section 27 requires the breeder to deposit the specified seed or propagating material, including applicable parental material, in the designated National Gene Bank under the regulations. These provisions help maintain identifiable reference material for protected varieties.

Seed availability matters because a useful variety benefits agriculture only when farmers can obtain suitable planting material. The Act therefore balances breeder protection with other provisions concerning farmer seed use and access to varieties.

Researcher's rights: the main exception

Section 30 specifically protects researcher's rights. It permits use of a registered variety for experiments or research and permits use of a variety as an initial source for developing other varieties.

There is an important qualification: breeder authorisation is required when repeated use of the registered variety as a parental line is necessary for commercial production of another newly developed variety.

Understanding the distinction

A researcher studying the characteristics of a registered variety may use it for experimental work under section 30. A breeder may also use the variety as an initial source when developing another variety. However, if producing the new commercial variety requires repeated use of the protected variety as a parental line, the relevant authorisation becomes necessary.

How long does registration last?

Section 24(6) distinguishes the initial certificate period from the maximum total period of protection. Renewal is required for the remaining eligible period, subject to the applicable requirements.

Variety categoryInitial certificate periodMaximum total period
Trees and vines9 years18 years from registration
Other crops6 yearsGenerally 15 years from registration
Extant varieties notified under section 5 of the Seeds Act, 19666 years for non-tree crops; 9 years for trees and vines15 years from the relevant Central Government notification under section 5 of the Seeds Act, 1966

The first 2 rows describe the initial periods by crop type; the third highlights the special statutory starting point for the maximum term of an extant variety notified under section 5 of the Seeds Act, 1966. The periods should not simply be added together.

Infringement and legal remedies

Unauthorised commercial production or sale of a registered variety may infringe the right, subject to the law's exemptions. Misleading use of the denomination of another registered variety may also constitute infringement.

Under sections 65–66, the entitled party can bring a civil infringement suit before a court of competent jurisdiction not below the level of a District Court. Relief may include an injunction and, subject to the court's determination, damages or a share of profits. These rights remain subject to the statutory protections for farmers and researchers.

Prelims focus

  • Section 28 sets out rights arising from registration of a plant variety.
  • Section 30 protects experimental and research use.
  • Repeated use of a protected variety as a parental line for commercial production requires breeder authorisation.
  • Section 24(6) provides an initial 9-year term for trees and vines and 6 years for other crops.
  • The maximum period is generally 18 years for trees and vines and 15 years for other cases, subject to the special rule for notified extant varieties.
  • Trap: The initial registration term is not always the maximum total period of protection.

[Sources: India Code, Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001, sections 24, 27–30 and 64–66, consulted 14 November 2026; Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Authority, 'Procedure in Case of Default/Recovery of Annual/Renewal Fees', section on renewal periods, consulted 14 November 2026; NCERT, Science, Class 9, 'Improvement in Food Resources', section 15.1.1, printed pp. 203–205.]

pictures.alt: Section 30 permits research and initial-source use; repeated parental-line use necessary for commercial production requires breeder authorisation.
pictures.caption: Research use is protected, but repeated parental-line use for commercial production has a specific condition.

title: Breeders' Rights, Researchers' Rights and the Duration of Variety Protection
